title: The Dullest Stocks in America

beats.text: The dullest stocks in America made one man a fortune.
Nineteen forty-seven. You're Shelby Davis, thirty-eight, a former insurance regulator.
You take your wife's fifty thousand dollars and buy insurance stocks.
Insurance. The most unloved corner of the market.
By nineteen fifty, they sell for four times earnings.
So how does boring make you rich?
You see, it's an apple orchard. First, the trees grow more apples.
Then apples come into fashion, and every apple sells for more.
Davis called it the double play.
Ten years later, insurers sold for fifteen to twenty times earnings.
Rich? He still scribbled notes on old envelopes.
By nineteen ninety-four, fifty thousand had become nine hundred million.
He didn't buy exciting stocks. He bought them before they were exciting.

facts.claim: Shelby Cullom Davis (1909-1994) started his investment firm in 1947 at age 38 with $50,000 provided by his wife Kathryn
Before that he was New York's First Deputy Superintendent of Insurance (1944-1947), a state insurance regulator
Insurance was an unloved sector; in 1950 insurers sold for about 4x earnings, ten years later 15-20x
Davis Double Play: a boost from growing earnings and another from investors bidding up the multiple
He was famously frugal and wrote notes on the backs of envelopes
By his death in 1994 the $50,000 had become about $900 million
The apple orchard is an analogy, not a historical scene

caption:
1947: $50,000 into the most unloved stocks in America — insurance companies at about 4x earnings.
Earnings grew. Then the market paid 15-20x for them. Shelby Davis called it the double play.
